papers.title: Bridging the QC–QA Cognitive Handoff: An Agentic Verification Harness for Error Detection, Specification Cross-Checking and Quality Documentation Assembly in Pharmaceutical Quality Assurance
papers.summary: Abstract Background. Quality control (QC) results reach regulatory dossiers through manual transcription and review. Such a benchmark does not yet exist. No collection of pharmaceutical quality documents carries discrepancies of known class and location, so automated verification cannot yet be evaluated against measured performance across realistic transfer errors and document types. Objectives. To specify (i) an architecture in which large language models only read and propose values, deterministic code performs every calculation and acceptance test, and a qualified reviewer makes every decision; (ii) a protocol for building a reference corpus and evaluating such systems; and (iii) sensitivity estimates from three dossiers. The plan covers design, evaluation, and measurement. Methods. Records from three ASEAN Common Technical Dossier Part II submissions (13, 14 and 10 records) were de-identified, and 112, 100 and 120 discrepancies across nine classes were introduced into dossiers A, B and C. A finding counted as a detection when it identified an injected discrepancy at the correct location with the correct class. The framework ran blind to the register. Sensitivity to injected discrepancies is reported per dossier with Wilson 95% confidence intervals and pooled by random-effects meta-analysis; clustering within records is not accounted for. Results. papers.title: Evidence constrained agentic retrieval augmented generation for substation civil engineering preliminary design documents in a single project study
papers.summary: Abstract Substation civil engineering preliminary design documents must integrate project-specific conditions, current regulatory requirements, typical design practices, and historical engineering experience while maintaining consistency across architectural, structural, general-layout, foundation, road, drainage, and technical-indicator sections. Conventional Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems remain vulnerable to condition-insensitive retrieval, unequal source authority, incompatible evidence, unsupported engineering claims, and parameter drift during long-document drafting. This study proposes an Evidence-Constrained Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework, termed EC-ARAG. The framework combines regulation-aware evidence representation, validity-gated hybrid retrieval, source-role-aware conflict resolution, dual planning--retrieval and generation--verification--repair loops, and global project-state memory. The experimental corpus comprised 36 national and industry standards, 12 enterprise standards, 18 typical-design documents, 64 historical preliminary design documents, and nine project-input documents. The held-out evaluation included 120 retrieval queries, 80 applicability cases, 48 evidence-conflict cases, 318 atomic design propositions, and five independent generation runs. papers.title: Safe Recovery of AI Agents in Enterprise Systems: Preventing Duplicate Actions and Preserving Human Corrections
papers.summary: Reliable use of AI agents in enterprise systems depends on what happens after an action fails or its outcome becomes uncertain. Retrying can duplicate an order, while reversing a workflow can invalidate a person’s subsequent correction. The central challenge is deciding whether recovery is justified by the available evidence and still satisfies the business request. We investigate this challenge in a reproducible testbed connecting order, inventory and billing services with different API guarantees. Controlled failures and concurrent edits reveal two evaluation gaps: protecting individual records does not ensure consistency across related services, and preserving an edit does not ensure that the final workflow fulfils its instruction. A separate diagnostic identified nine apparent completions that left human instructions unsatisfied. A conventional recovery implementation with equivalent safeguards matched the evaluated controller in all 270 paired runs, locating the observed benefit in shared engineering protections rather than a distinct recovery algorithm. On the prospective test configurations, both completed 108 of 180 runs without scored violations and left 72 for manual resolution. These findings provide a practical basis for evaluating agent integrations: verify uncertain effects, check related records, and distinguish completed business goals from unresolved handoffs.

papers.title: ARES OS 2.0: An Orchestration Software Suite for Autonomous Experimentation Systems and Self-Driving Labs
papers.summary: ARES OS 2.0 (hereinafter ARES OS) is an open-source software suite to enable laboratory automation and closed-loop autonomous experimentation. Its function is to orchestrate experimental actions and data handoff between lab equipment, analysis routines, and experimental planning modules through a service-oriented architecture. ARES OS is abstracted to apply to general experimental flows common in materials science, chemistry, and biology and related disciplines. The core of ARES OS provides central control over all modules, along with the heavy lifting of UI creation, data management, and experimental design tools. ARES OS modules communicate with the core software over protobuf and gRPC, allowing them to be language-agnostic and user-creatable. This allows users to easily implement modules that control experimental hardware, process collected data , or plan experiments to meet their specific research needs. ARES OS lowers the barrier to entry for researchers to build their own self-driving labs, allowing them to focus on scientific programming for their use case and reducing the effort and time needed to bring an autonomous experimentation system online.

papers.title: vibyverse: an integrated computational chemistry ecosystem developed through agentic engineering
papers.summary: We describe the vibyverse, developed by agentic engineering, comprising vibe-sketcher for chemical structures and reaction schemes, vibe-qc for electronic-structure calculations, vibe-scheduler for execution and retrieval, vibe-viewer for inspection and presentation, and the Quantum Visualization Format (QVF) for structured exchange. The workflow starts with reaction design in vibe-sketcher, submission through vibe-scheduler, calculation with vibe-qc, and inspection and analysis in vibe-viewer, with scientific data transferred through QVF. We examine the responsibilities of each component and the information that must survive their connections, including charge, multiplicity, geometry, method settings, runtime identity and result provenance. Source inspection identifies implemented interfaces and their compatibility requirements. A Diels–Alder preparation example connects an editable scheme and preoptimized structures to validated QVF and viewer exports. The executed numerical workflow proceeds through MACE geometry optimization, PBE/def2-SVP refinement and DLPNO-CCSD(T) endpoint energies. A proposed water-on-boronnitride example would extend the workflow to periodic structures. The molecular optimization and Hessian use existing PBE routes without an added dispersion correction. Both Hessian stencils identify minima for all three molecules. With an explicit restrictedreference

papers.title: MetaNav: Metacognitive Vision-Language Navigation via Reflective Exploration
papers.summary: Training-free Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) agents powered by foundation models can follow instructions and explore 3D environments. However, existing approaches rely on greedy frontier selection and passive spatial memory, leading to inefficient behaviors such as local oscillation and redundant revisiting. We argue that this stems from a lack of metacognitive capabilities: the agent cannot monitor its exploration progress, diagnose strategy failures, or adapt accordingly. To address this, we propose MetaNav, a metacognitive navigation agent integrating spatial memory, history-aware planning, and reflective correction. Spatial memory builds a persistent 3D semantic map. History-aware planning penalizes revisiting to improve efficiency. Reflective correction detects stagnation and uses an LLM to generate corrective rules that guide future frontier selection. Experiments on GOAT-Bench, HM3D-OVON, and A-EQA show that MetaNav achieves state-of-the-art performance while reducing VLM queries by 20.7%, demonstrating that metacognitive reasoning significantly improves robustness and efficiency. The code is available at https://github.com/perfectlxy7/MetaNav.

papers.title: Supporting engagement, behavior change, and equitable self-management in menstrual and menopausal health: A multi-agent digital-health framework
papers.summary: Menstrual-cycle-related conditions and, later, menopausal symptoms are highly prevalent across the female life course and impose a large, under-recognized burden on quality of life and work, yet digital tools to support self-management are fragmented, hard to sustain, and unevenly reached. We propose HERA (Health Engagement and Reflective Agent architecture), a conceptual, hypothesis-generating framework for supporting engagement, behavior change, and equitable self-management in menstrual and menopausal health across the life course. Under human governance, HERA combines two adaptive agents (interpretation and orchestration) with three rule-based modules (self-monitoring and data integration, guidance and content governance, and equity and engagement monitoring) that integrate self-monitoring, deliver personalized feedback, surface governed guidance, monitor equity, and coordinate hand-offs to clinicians and occupational-health services. Distinct from clinician-facing diagnostic agents, HERA is patient-facing and treats equity and engagement as first-class. We distinguish technically feasible from aspirational elements and set out a staged, threshold-gated evaluation plan. HERA is a design reference, not a validated system.

papers.title: Learning‐by‐twinning: Organizational digital twins and the future of search
papers.summary: Abstract Research Summary Entrepreneurs and managers often need to evaluate strategic choices, such as redesigning an incentive plan or entering an unfamiliar market, before committing scarce resources. Existing offline search tools, including mental models, analogical reasoning, model building, and simulation, allow managers to weigh alternatives without acting, but each is limited by what a single decision maker can specify, recall, or imagine. We argue that advances in generative AI, combined with the growing availability of firm‐specific digital trace data, are transforming this tradeoff. We introduce the organizational digital twin (ODT), an infrastructure combining firm‐specific data, AI‐based behavioral simulation models, and governance rules which facilitates a new form of offline search that we call learning‐by‐twinning: search conducted by observing how a strategic choice unfolds within a digital replica of the firm. We identify three mechanisms through which learning‐by‐twinning creates value, namely expanded search, safer experimentation, and richer system‐level feedback as well as specify certain conditions under which these benefits may attenuate. Managerial Summary Strategic entrepreneurship depends on discovering and refining opportunities through search and experimentation under uncertainty. papers.title: Digital-Twin-Driven Predictive Maintenance and Fault-Tolerant Control for Electrified Agricultural Machinery: A Multiphysics and Deep Reinforcement Learning Framework for PMSM In-Wheel Drives
papers.summary: Electrified agricultural machinery increasingly relies on permanent-magnet synchronous motor drives that must remain dependable under variable traction, terrain-induced vibration, thermal cycling, contamination, and intermittent duty. Existing work offers mature methods for motor fault diagnosis, digital twins, predictive maintenance, and distributed-drive fault-tolerant control, but their health information is often not shared across diagnosis, maintenance, and control. This article develops a multiphysics digital-twin framework in which electrical, thermal, mechanical, and vibrational evidence maintains a probabilistic health belief that constrains both supervisory maintenance decisions and torque redistribution. The framework formalizes observability, uncertainty-aware health factors, deterministic safety shielding, multi-rate fallback logic, and agriculture-specific traction constraints. Reproducible low-fidelity numerical studies provide preliminary support for context-conditioned residual diagnosis and the revised thermal-continuity trade-off underlying health-aware derating, including robustness and sensitivity analyses. They do not validate sim-to-real transfer or the reinforcement-learning policy itself; those hypotheses remain open for dynamometer and hardware-in-the-loop testing. The results are therefore interpreted as mechanism-level evidence rather than field-perf

papers.title: Exploring or Exploiting Generative AI? A Dual-Path, Dual-Horizon Theory of Employee Incremental and Radical Creativity
papers.summary: Recent research has established that generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is not a unitary workplace resource: exploratory and exploitative use orientations are associated with different forms of employee creativity, and their value depends on employees' capacity to integrate generated knowledge. This article therefore does not present the basic dual path as a new discovery. Instead, it develops a theoretical integration and dynamic extension that asks why the established paths operate differently, when employees should switch between them, and how short-run augmentation can evolve into either capability accumulation or capability substitution. We distinguish expansive and consolidative modes of knowledge integration, theorize phase-congruent switching rather than static ``high-high'' ambidexterity, and position metacognition as a control mechanism that governs both immediate knowledge conversion and longer-run cognitive development. We further specify cultural tightness and psychological safety as directional boundary conditions and distinguish individual creative gains from collective idea-space diversity. The framework converts emerging empirical regularities into falsifiable propositions about task phase, context, and time, providing a research agenda for sustainable human--AI creativity.

papers.title: Can TDD improve the quality of LLM-migrated code? : A pilot study in an industrial context
papers.summary: The emergence of Large Language Models (LLM) has created new possibilities for automating software development, yet ensuring the quality of AI-generated code remains a major challenge. We aim to investigate if Test-Driven Development (TDD) can improve the quality of code generated by an LLM in a fully autonomous context, within a pilot project at Decerno AB. We added TDD to their pilot workflow, using a design science approach, with continuous refinements to prompt design and workflow structure, based on observed AI behavior. The generated code was evaluated and compared with non-TDD code, using SonarQube for static code analysis. The results indicate that TDD reduced complexity and code duplication, but introduced more quality issues overall, while non-TDD produced fewer, but more severe issues. The generated tests from the TDD workflow focused more on content verification than on behavioral testing, contributing to a lower code coverage per test compared to non-TDD. The findings suggest that TDD involves trade-offs that may favor certain development priorities, in particular where lower complexity and reduced duplication are more beneficial than minimizing total issue count. This indicates that a strict application of TDD may not be optimal in an autonomous AI-driven context, and that exploring more flexible adaptations of the TDD workflow remains interesting for future resea

papers.title: From Coding to Creativity: Integrating Design Thinking into IT and Technology Education
papers.summary: This study examines how the integration of Design Thinking into Information Technology (IT) and technology education can bridge technical programming skills and creative, human-centered problem-solving. Specifically, it explores how the five stages of Design Thinking empathizing, defining, ideating, prototyping, and testing shape students’ creative thinking, active engagement, and collaborative learning experiences. A qualitative research approach was employed, involving teachers, students, and school principals as key informants. Data were collected through in-depth interviews, classroom observations, and documentation of learning activities, then analyzed thematically to identify recurring patterns in teaching practices and student experiences. The findings indicate that Design Thinking creates opportunities for students to move beyond coding procedures toward developing digital solutions that respond to real users’ needs. Through collaborative ideation, iterative prototyping, and feedback-based testing, students demonstrate greater involvement in learning, explore alternative solutions, and communicate their ideas more actively. The approach also provides opportunities to develop empathy, creativity, collaboration, and a willingness to experiment with and revise initial designs. papers.title: Exercise enhances cancer immunotherapy by reshaping systemic T cell homeostasis
papers.summary: Although immune checkpoint inhibitors have revolutionized cancer treatment, therapeutic resistance and heterogeneous patient responses remain major clinical challenges. Current paradigms predominantly focus on amplifying effector T cells (Teffs); however, this approach frequently encounters structural bottlenecks imposed by a tumor-locked, suppressive immune homeostasis. Central to this aberrant equilibrium are regulatory T cells (Tregs), which persistently elevate immune activation thresholds and restrict durable antitumor responses. In this review, we propose a paradigm shift toward reshaping baseline T cell homeostasis, highlighting exercise as a potent, systemic physiological intervention. Regular exercise systematically counteracts tumor-induced homeostatic locking by reprogramming immune metabolism, attenuating chronic inflammation, and improving tissue perfusion. Rather than indiscriminately depleting Tregs, exercise dynamically recalibrates the Teff/Treg balance, lowering activation thresholds while preserving systemic immune tolerance. Furthermore, we propose that structured physical activity may support a form of “homeostatic memory,” with potential implications for the durability of immunotherapy responses. Integrating exercise into oncological care offers a translational, host-centered strategy to optimize the immune background, thereby unlocking the full clinical p

papers.title: A Comprehensive Review of AI and IoT-Based Water Pipeline Leakage Detection, Prediction and Monitoring Systems
papers.summary: Water pipeline leakage is a major challenge in water distribution and supply systems because undetected leaks can result in water loss, infrastructure damage, economic losses, and inefficient water management [5], [13]. Conventional leakage inspection methods often depend on manual inspection, periodic maintenance, or specialized equipment, which may not provide continuous real-time monitoring [5], [13]. Recent developments in the Internet of Things (IoT), sensor technology, artificial intelligence (AI), and machine learning (ML) have created opportunities for automated and intelligent pipeline monitoring [9], [11]. This review presents a study of recent techniques used for water pipeline leakage detection, localization, prediction, and monitoring. Different sensing approaches, including flow, pressure, acoustic, and vibration measurements, are reviewed along with machine-learning and deep-learning methods [1], [3], [4], [8], [12], [13]. Existing research demonstrates that pressure and flow measurements are widely used for hydraulic anomaly detection, while vibration and acoustic measurements can provide additional information about leakage events [5], [6], [7]. papers.title: Climate ODER: Information, Coordination, and the Time to Act
papers.summary: An accurate forecast can leave a response team without a usable basis for timely protection. Climate ODER, developed through Observer-Dependent Entropy Retrieval, asks what information must survive, who must retain it, and when it must be secured. In a finite model, available information supports a task when every group of indistinguishable records admits a common acceptable action. As protective options expire, a distinction can become necessary after its last timely recovery opportunity has closed. We establish this separation between preservation and action deadlines. An exact access-locator frontier shows that two initial categories can support timely recovery where immediate action requires arbitrarily many target categories. The recovered answer still carries the target information. A temporal preservation criterion constructs the distinctions that make intermediate recovery operations and final protective choices executable under a specified causal memory mechanism. Extensions give exact criteria for unequal consultation times and a declared class of monotone response rules. For distributed response, we characterize failures of shared-plan selection even when each participant’s information is individually sufficient, construct minimum-cost feature repairs, and derive their budget–deadline frontier under specified acquisition conditions. papers.title: Metacognitive Reasoning in Energy Based Models Using Instance Based Learning Theory
papers.summary: Metacognition involves reasoning about cognitive processes themselves. An example is in resource allocation where we choose how much time and effort to put into a reasoning task before we begin based on our confidence. Current Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems that rely on Large Language Models (LLMs) cannot estimate their uncertainty about an output without first responding, and cannot dynamically allocate resources to producing an output, making this type of metacognitive process difficult. A recently proposed alternative to classic transformer architectures that addresses these two concerns is the Energy Based Model (EBM) which allows for interpretable uncertainty modeling and dynamic allocation of compute resources. While EBMs can allow for control of these two processes, the actual metacognitive task of determining compute allocation based on uncertainty is not directly addressed. Instance-Based Learning Theory (IBLT) provides an approach to modeling human-like decisions from experience that has previously been applied to predicting human metacognitive reasoning. In this paper we introduce a framework for MEtacognitive Reasoning with Instance-based Learning Theory and Energy Dynamics (MERITED). Grounded in IBLT, this framework allows for control of the computational effort allocated in an EBM to allow for metacognitive control over reasoning effort based on uncertainty

papers.title: Refining collaborative AI literacy: A systematic review of human–AI collaboration competency and AI literacy measures
papers.summary: With the widespread adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) and its growing role in solving complex problems, human–AI interaction has evolved into a new dimension, where AI is increasingly perceived as a collaborative partner. However, current AI literacy frameworks focus on technical knowledge and ethical use, often neglecting the ability to collaborate effectively with AI as a standalone construct. Conceptualized under the umbrella of AI literacy, the boundaries of human–AI collaboration competency need to be refined in order to create common ground for advancing research and measurement of this essential ability. This systematic review synthesizes 17 studies conducted in higher education settings to examine how human–AI collaboration competency is represented and measured within existing AI literacy scales. The findings reveal that human–AI collaboration is rarely explicitly assessed, let alone as a distinct construct. Some studies included a small number of items that could implicitly refer to collaboration competency or context, but most included no such representation. Drawing on these findings, we propose theoretical implications regarding contexts and factors that should be considered when developing new items, and measurement implications for three possible sub-factors of human–AI collaboration competency: coordination, communication, and metacognition. papers.title: Interactive Digital Media-Assisted SSCS Learning: A Solution to Enhance Problem-Solving Ability and Alleviate Mathematics Anxiety
papers.summary: Problem-solving is a practical skill that students must master in 21st-century learning. However, various findings indicate that this capability remains low among junior high school students, who are beginning to study mathematical concepts in greater depth. Anxiety toward the subject matter, teachers, and mathematics instruction itself is a key factor influencing students' mathematical problem-solving performance. To address this, this study aims to examine the effect of the Search, Solve, Create, and Share (SSCS) learning model, a model that provides a clear roadmap for students to implement Polya's problem-solving steps, assisted by interactive digital media (PhET and Mathigon), on students' problem-solving ability and anxiety. This quasi-experimental study used a factorial design and included eighth-grade students. The research sample was selected using the cluster random sampling technique. Data were collected using a test instrument and a mathematics anxiety questionnaire and were subsequently analyzed using a two-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA). The results of the study indicate that: (1) Hypothesis testing showed that there was a significant effect of different learning models on students’ problem-solving ability, with Fobs (= 8.405) > Ftab (= 4.016). papers.title: Video and digital games: Historical controversies, benefits, and risks for children and adolescents
papers.summary: Video and digital games have been the focus of sustained public and scientific debate since their commercial emergence in the late 1970s, particularly regarding their effects on children and adolescents. Early public and scientific discourse frequently portrayed gaming as a source of physical injury, addiction, aggression, social isolation, academic problems, and moral decline. However, subsequent empirical research has produced a substantially more differentiated picture of both the benefits and risks of gaming. This review examines the historical foundations of controversies surrounding video and digital games and synthesizes contemporary evidence concerning their cognitive, emotional, social, therapeutic, and physical effects. . Research indicates that moderate, purposeful gaming may improve visuospatial abilities, attentional control, problem-solving, mood regulation, social connection, and selected educational outcomes. Gaming-based interventions have also demonstrated therapeutic potential, particularly for depressive symptoms and attention-related difficulties among young people. At the same time, important risks remain, especially when gaming becomes excessive, compulsive, or disruptive to everyday functioning. These include repetitive-strain injuries, sleep disruption, problematic gaming, and adverse mental-health and academic outcomes. Evidence concerning violent game

papers.title: An Assessment of Accessibility and Affordability of Inpatient Psychiatric Care in Tennessee
papers.summary: Introduction: Access to mental health has seen changes over the past decade, but little research and attention have been given to access to inpatient psychiatric facilities. Inpatient psychiatric care is crucial for patients experiencing mental health emergencies who need immediate access to care. Gaps in spatial accessibility, affordability, and the access and assessment process were identified due to a lack of available information in the field. Methods: Secondary data from the Tennessee Department of Health were used to assess financial accessibility through payer source charges and patient encounters, as well as through mapping of inpatient psychiatric facilities and conducting drive time and coverage area analyses. Primary data were collected through interviews with clinicians located in Northeastern Tennessee to gain insight into the assessment process and gather their perceptions of inpatient care. Results: Longitudinal descriptive reviews on the financial accessibility among Tennessee Inpatient Facilities. This showed increased variability among facilities when stratified by region, ownership, and type of operation. Spatial accessibility in ArcGIS showed 82% of counties were not covered within a 30-minute radius of inpatient facilities. papers.title: Pieces Solving a Puzzle: Emerging Roles and Cross-Field Analogies During a Distributed Epistemic Game
papers.summary: In an effort to describe why some problems can’t be solved, a character compared them to a cubic meter of platinum - a block so dense that all the people who could squeeze around it still couldn’t lift it off the ground. In the same way, these problems simply can’t have enough people gathered around and communicating about them - and so they remain unsolved. This research looks at the first Polymath Project (2009) as an example of a distributed epistemic game to examine how groups engage with complex problems. and without a locally omniscient individual. In this setting of epistemic uncertainty, interactions between individuals reveal patterns of participation, and an analogy opens a new solution pathway by introducing a problem-solving approach from another field. These insights answer the initial question of the Polymath Project - ‘Is massively collaborative mathematics possible?’ - and offer hope for lifting the cubic meter of other unsolvable problems.

papers.title: Designing a Curriculum Model Based on Artificial Intelligence and Purposeful Physical Activity to Enhance Learning Self-Regulation, Mental Health, and Psychological Well-Being among Students
papers.summary: Objective: The objective of this study was to design and validate a curriculum model based on artificial intelligence and purposeful physical activity with emphasis on enhancing learning self-regulation, mental health, and psychological well-being among students. Methods and Materials: This applied developmental study was conducted using an exploratory sequential mixed-methods design. In the qualitative phase, 20 experts in curriculum studies, educational technology, artificial intelligence in education, physical education, educational psychology, and student mental health were selected through purposive criterion-based sampling from Tehran and participated in semi-structured interviews. The interview data were analyzed using thematic analysis to extract the main dimensions, components, and indicators of the proposed curriculum model. In the quantitative phase, 384 secondary school students from Tehran were selected through multistage cluster sampling during the 2025–2026 academic year. Data were collected using a researcher-made curriculum model validation questionnaire, a learning self-regulation questionnaire, the General Health Questionnaire, and a psychological well-being scale. papers.title: AI & Cognitive Work
papers.summary: Artificial systems now perform a striking range of cognitive tasks. This Element defends three claims. First, the status quo for cognitive work cannot survive. Whatever AI's trajectory, the package of features defining cognitive work – high skill requirements, credentials, wage premiums, resistance to automation, and low productivity growth – will be radically transformed. Second, the widespread displacement of humans from cognitive work, though it sounds alarming, may pose no special threat to human flourishing. Whatever makes work good for people is equally available outside cognitive work, and displacement enables leveraged gains in research and access to justice. Third, a world of ubiquitous cognitive assistance, though it sounds benign, carries distinctive moral risks, especially for children. Cognitive assistance works by reducing cognitive difficulty. But cognitive difficulty is necessary for the normal development of executive function – the capacities constitutive of autonomous agency. This title is also available as Open Access on Cambridge Core.

papers.title: Understanding the Neurobiology of Heart Rate Variability: Central, Peripheral, and Developmental Contributions in Rodents
papers.summary: The study of heart rate variability has grown rapidly in popularity in the age of smart technology, however this growth at the cutting edge has progressed without the necessary foundational understanding of the complexities. Rodent modelling of HRV allows for the experimental testing of underlying mechanisms to build a strong foundation for future studies in HRV, however, current rodent experiments are limited and lacking in methodological consistency. The first chapter of this thesis will provide a theoretical overview of HRV from early foundational concepts, up to the current theoretical models, while providing a strong foundation usable to those new to the field of HRV and experts alike. Chapter two provides a data driven methodology for the study of HRV in rats, from a detailed surgical procedure through to the transparent analysis and reporting of essential parameters. Chapter three examines the contributions of the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous system to many of the common parameters of HRV using centrally acting and peripherally isolated pharmacological blockades. Chapter four explores the central regulation of HRV through the manipulation of GABA in the infralimbic prefrontal cortex via intracerebral infusions of muscimol and bicuculine. papers.title: Biomaterials in 3D bioprinting: Design strategies, material-technique interactions, and biomedical applications
papers.summary: Three-dimensional (3D) bioprinting has emerged as a transformative approach in biomedical engineering, enabling the fabrication of complex, patient-specific constructs through layer-by-layer deposition of biomaterials and living cells. This review critically synthesizes the role of biomaterials in 3D bioprinting by comparing how material properties, fabrication techniques, and biological requirements interact to determine construct performance across different biomedical applications. Unlike many existing reviews that discuss materials, techniques, and applications separately, this review focuses on the coupled interactions between biomaterial chemistry, fabrication methods, and application-specific requirements across multiple tissue systems. Across these applications, no single biomaterial satisfies all design requirements, leading to compromises between mechanical strength, printability, and biological performance. Hard tissue applications prioritize thermoplastic polymers and ceramics for structural integrity, while soft tissue engineering relies on hydrogel-based bioinks. Printing techniques such as extrusion, inkjet, and stereolithography impose constraints related to resolution, viscosity, and cell viability, driving the use of composite biomaterials and hybrid fabrication strategies. papers.title: Multi-omics and machine learning reveal a senescence-associated lipid-metabolic macrophage phenotype driving immunosuppression and poor prognosis in colorectal cancer
papers.summary: Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) are key regulators of the tumor microenvironment in colorectal cancer (CRC), yet their functional heterogeneity remains poorly understood, especially regarding the interplay between cellular senescence and lipid metabolism. We integrated multi-omics and single-cell transcriptomic data to characterize a novel macrophage subpopulation termed senescence-associated lipid-metabolic (SALM) macrophages. Using eight machine learning algorithms, a prognostic model based on SALM signatures was developed and internally evaluated via nested cross-validation in a combined TCGA–GSE39582 cohort. Spatial multiplex immunofluorescence and qPCR were employed for experimental validation. SALM macrophages exhibit elevated IL-10/STAT3 signaling, terminal differentiation, and a core gene module enriched in senescence and lipid metabolism pathways. They interact strongly with T cells via immunosuppressive ligands IL-10 and MIF. Spatial analysis confirmed p16 + CD68 + IL-10 + cell enrichment at the tumor front. The SALM-based prognostic model achieved high accuracy (AUC = 0.972), and a corresponding nomogram showed potential for personalized prognosis prediction. SALM macrophages drive immunosuppression in CRC through a senescence-lipid metabolism axis, serving as a novel prognostic biomarker and potential therapeutic target.

papers.title: De Novo Design of Catalytically Active Salen-Binding Proteins
papers.summary: Abstract De novo design of catalytic metalloproteins has the potential to generate enzymes that combine the efficiency of natural proteins with the reactivity of synthetic organometallic catalysts. Here, we develop a computational strategy to design enzymes with novel tertiary structures that bind metal salen complexes, classic small-molecule catalysts not found in biology. Six proteins were designed and screened for function; five of six express well, bind a Co-salen cofactor, and catalyze a transition metal hydrogen atom transfer (MHAT)-mediated deallylation reaction, representing the first de novo proteins to catalyze this class of transformation. The spectroscopic properties and crystal structure of the most active sequence were in excellent agreement with the design, and the holoprotein retained its structure and activity over a broad range of pH (2–12), temperatures up to 95 °C, and aqueous/organic solvent mixtures. We suggest that the combinatorial space provided by metal ion identity, ligand substitution, and active site structure can be used to generate artificial metalloenzymes that catalyze many chemical transformations.
